title: Thursday's Three Things—Resources, Reasoning, and Restraint
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
source: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning (Substack), August 6, 2026
summary: This is the final 'Thursday's Three Things' of the summer from Episcopal Academy's Center for Teaching and Learning, structured as three curated items with real editorial commentary. 'Resources' points teachers to Holly Korbey's Bell Ringer newsletter 'Back-to-School Companion.' 'Reasoning' summarizes a study by Abigail Baird, Jonathan Fugelsang, and Craig Bennett on the uneven brain networks behind adolescent decision-making. The third item, 'Restraint,' examines a study (reviewed by Pedro De Bruyckere) on AI use by teachers, whose key finding is that benefits to teachers don't automatically translate into benefits for students — AI should support, not replace, pedagogical thinking.
points: Curates three teacher-facing resources under 'Resources, Reasoning, and Restraint.'
Points to Holly Korbey's Bell Ringer 'Back-to-School Companion' as a deeper resource than the CTL could compile itself.
Highlights research (Baird, Fugelsang, Bennett) on adolescent brain networks that may leave students vulnerable to poor in-the-moment decisions.
Summarizes a study reviewed by Pedro De Bruyckere finding AI benefits for teachers don't automatically transfer to benefits for students.
Closes with a caution that AI should support, not replace, pedagogical thinking.
quotes: This is the final Thursday's Three Things for the summer as we take a hiatus next week before ramping up our weekly Wednesday writing for the school year.
but then Holly Korbey's The Bell Ringer Substack comes along and drops its 'Back-to-School Companion' which dwarfs anything we might compile in the coming weeks.

This study from Abigail Baird, Jonathan Fugelsang, and Craig Bennett highlights the varied capabilities for adolescents when it comes to decision making and the inefficient brain networks that 'may leave them vulnerable to poor decision making.'
Evidence suggests 'that benefits for teachers do not automatically become benefits for students.'
AI can reduce administrative work, provide inspiration and help with routine tasks. But when it starts to replace pedagogical thinking rather than support it, genuine risks may emerge.
If we want our students to think, let's not offload our own thinking along the way.
